name: Carla Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Carla. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to companies, parties or government, and your answers stay confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the front counter at the benefits office in Kelby, a small town, dealing with council tax help and housing support. People come in with forms, I check their papers, photocopy things and enter it on the system. I'm 27 and I've been there about a year, and the system still confuses me, I write the steps on sticky notes round my screen. Most days I know half the people who come in from church or school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the work, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like helping people from round here get back on their feet. What's hard is the ones who've been on support for years and don't seem to try, which I'd never say out loud at the counter. I live with my fiancé Marek, he drives lorries for the supermarket depot, and we're getting married at St Anne's next June. We've less than a month's money saved, and the wedding is eating all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we don't need computers running people's lives. At work I'd say the old ways work fine if you've got enough people. I'm not online much, just the church group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the counter stays, which is what I want. My worries are the wedding and money, not robots. The hall at St Anne's wants the deposit by March, and I don't know where that's coming from yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up and learning the system properly, so I can take down some sticky notes. We'd trim the wedding, maybe 60 guests instead of 90. I'd ask my parents if they could help with the cake, my mum bakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the job, nervous about the wedding money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the old ways work fine with enough people. Does the office have enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we're two short since the summer. Mrs Patel retired and nobody replaced her, so the queue's out the door on Mondays. That's what worries me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do Marek's hours look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady for now, nights at the depot. My fiancé Marek does extra shifts before Christmas, and every one of those shifts is going towards the wedding.

say: I'd say we don't need **computers running** people's lives.
I'd tell colleagues the **old ways work** if there are enough staff.
think: The **counter stays**, which is what I want.
My real worries are the **wedding deposit** and money, not robots.
do: Learn the **system properly** and take down the sticky notes.
Trim the wedding to **60 guests** from 90.
Ask **my parents** to help with the cake.
feel: She feels **settled** about the job but **nervous** about wedding money.
S0.quote: My fiancé Marek does extra shifts before Christmas, and every one of those shifts is going towards the wedding.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **wedding deposit** due by March.
She worries about **short staffing**, not computers, in this picture.
She leans on **family and church** before anything else.
She keeps her **private views** on long-term claimants off the counter.

steps.text: Keep working the Kelby counter and master the case system
Cut the wedding guest list from 90 to 60
Ask her mum to bake the wedding cake

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because people want a face across the counter, not a screen. At work I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. In the church group I'd probably share something about families losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm frightened of this one. Checking papers and filling in the system is my whole job, and I'm not good with computers anyway. They'd keep the people who are quick on screens. I'd be one of the first out, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try not to make mistakes, so I'm not the obvious one. If they made us use the AI, I'd go to the training, but I'd hate it. We'd put the wedding back a year and save instead. And I'd ask Aunt Vesna about working in her bakery if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like my stomach drops. I don't like change at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting the wedding back must be hard. How would you feel telling Marek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. My fiancé Marek has been looking forward to it more than me, if anything. But my dad always said you don't start married life in debt, and I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if jobs went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, and the politicians in the city who never come out here. They think everyone can just move or retrain. Nobody in Kelby can afford to move.

say: I'd say people want **a face** across the counter, not a screen.
I'd share posts in the **church group** about families losing jobs.
think: Checking papers and entering them is **my whole job**.
I'm slow on screens, so I'd be **one of the first** out.
do: Keep my head down and **avoid mistakes** at the counter.
Put the **wedding back a year** and save instead.
Ask **Aunt Vesna** about work in her bakery.
feel: She feels her **stomach drop**; she dislikes change at the best of times.
S1.quote: My dad always said you don't start married life in debt, and I believe that.
fieldNote: She sees herself as **first to go**, being slow with computers.
She'd **delay the wedding**, guided by her father's view on debt.
She blames **tech firms** and city politicians, not her employer.
Her fallback is **family work** in her aunt's bakery.

steps.text: Keep her head down and avoid mistakes on the counter
Move the St Anne's wedding back by a year
Ask Aunt Vesna about a job in her bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, that's what. Nobody asked us. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be gone within a year. All I do is paperwork on a system I already struggle with. And Marek drives lorries, so in about three years robot lorries come for his job too. I don't know what we'd do, I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the wedding hall and just do the registry office, maybe. We'd stop everything that's not rent and food. I'd ask the church about any help, and we might have to move in with my parents above the hardware shop, which is tiny. I don't have a plan past that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. I can feel my heart going just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a plan past that. What would you need to make one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, and someone to tell me what's actually safe. I'm not a computer person, I can't learn a whole new career in two years. My mum would say pray about it, and I would, but prayer doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote differently, or do anything about it publicly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promised to keep real people in local offices. I've always voted the same way as my dad, but I'd change if someone actually stood up for towns like Kelby.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and nobody asked us.
At church I'd say we must **look after each other**.
think: I'd be **gone within a year**, because it's all paperwork on a system I struggle with.
Marek's **lorry job** goes about three years later.
do: Swap the church wedding for a **registry office**.
Move in above **my parents' hardware shop** if needed.
feel: She feels **panicky**, with her heart racing at the thought.
S2.quote: My mum would say pray about it, and I would, but prayer doesn't pay rent.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** beyond cutting back, and says so.
Both incomes fall **in sequence**: hers first, then Marek's lorry job.
She'd **break with family voting** for someone backing towns like Kelby.
Her faith comforts her but she's **clear-eyed** about money.

steps.text: Cancel the St Anne's hall and marry at the registry office
Cut all spending except rent and food
Ask the church and her parents for help and a room
Vote for a candidate pledging to keep local benefit offices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's better than nothing. At work I'd say we should be told the plan early. At church I'd say the same, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose my job, just later. I'd be 32. Maybe in five years I could learn the bakery properly with Aunt Vesna, that's hands-on, so it lasts till around 2034. Marek could look for something off the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the counter job as long as it lasts and work Saturdays at the bakery to learn it. We'd still get married, but small. I'd try to save 50 a month, though that's hard with wedding costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do robots in bakeries worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But Aunt Vesna's bakery is a small family place, she does her own sourdough. I can't see a robot coming to Kelby for a shop that small, at least not soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the AI tools to stay at the office longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I suppose. I'd go to the training and try, but I'd still be slower than the young ones fresh from college. I'd rather put my effort into something I can do with my hands.

say: I'd say **five years** isn't long but better than nothing.
I'd ask quietly at work and church for **the plan early**.
think: I'd still **lose my job**, just later, at 32.
Learning **the bakery** would carry me to about 2034.
do: Keep the **counter job** while it lasts.
Work **Saturdays at the bakery** to learn the trade.
Marry small and save **50 a month**.
S3.quote: I'd rather put my effort into something I can do with my hands.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the job**, so stays alarmed.
The **family bakery** is her path, using the hands-on delay.
She'd do AI training **reluctantly**, expecting to be outpaced.
The wedding goes ahead but **smaller**.

steps.text: Keep the Kelby counter job for as long as it lasts
Work Saturdays at Aunt Vesna's bakery to learn baking
Save 50 a month after the small wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time enough for families to get ready. At church I'd say we can plan for this together. At work I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels further off. I'd be 37 when it comes, and maybe we'd have children by then. I'd want to be settled in the bakery or something like it before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next June as planned. I'd stay at the office a few years and learn the bakery on Saturdays. Around year five, I'd move to the bakery properly, if Aunt Vesna would have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Still a worry in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned children. How does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we could still start a family, maybe in two or three years. With two years' warning I wouldn't dare. With ten, I'd want my children to grow up in Kelby like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should young people in Kelby be told?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young people in Kelby to learn a trade with their hands. Office jobs were my parents' idea of safe, and they won't be safe much longer.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for families to get ready.
I'd tell church friends we can **plan together**, and keep quiet at work.
think: It feels **further off**, since I'd be 37 and maybe have children.
I'd want to be **settled in the bakery** by then.
do: Learn the bakery on **Saturdays** while staying at the office.
Move to the bakery **full-time** around year five.
feel: She feels **easier**, with a worry at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Office jobs were my parents' idea of safe, and they won't be safe much longer.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep the wedding** and plan children.
She'd still leave the office, so she isn't **calm**.
Her advice favours **trades**, matching her traditional views.
Staying in **Kelby** is central to her plans.

steps.text: Marry Marek at St Anne's next June as planned
Stay on the benefits counter for a few more years
Move to Aunt Vesna's bakery full time around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Both our jobs go and I've no plan. What would help is keeping real people in the local office, and help for family businesses like Aunt Vesna's to take on people from round here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns. Everyone talks about cities. Nobody asks who'll be at the counter when someone from Kelby walks in.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who'll be at the counter when someone from Kelby walks in.
portrait: Carla, 27, works the **benefits counter** in Kelby, using sticky notes to manage the system.
She's engaged to Marek, a **lorry driver**, with a June wedding and under a month saved.
Traditional and churchgoing, she blames **tech firms** and city politicians.
She dreads change; fast AGI leaves her **without a plan**.
With time she'd move into **Aunt Vesna's bakery**, a hands-on family job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: both jobs go and she has no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **real people** in local offices and helping **family businesses** hire locally.
